design_detail: Double-blind, double-dummy, placebo-controlled randomized crossover trial (balanced 4 × 4 Latin square), Institut Municipal d'Investigació Mèdica, Barcelona: 9 healthy men with prior recreational MDMA use each completed four 10-h outpatient sessions one week apart: MDMA 100 mg plus alcohol 0.8 g/kg; MDMA plus a placebo drink; placebo capsule plus alcohol; and double placebo. The drink (vodka and tonic, 350 ml, taken over 15 min) started 30 min after the capsules. Measures over 6–24 h: digit symbol substitution test (DSST), simple reaction time, Maddox wing (eye-muscle balance, used as a sign of sedation or stimulation), the 49-item Addiction Research Center Inventory (ARCI) and 23 visual analogue scales; plasma MDMA and blood alcohol. Peak change in the first 6 h and 6-h area under the curve analysed by repeated-measures ANOVA with Tukey tests; time course by two-way ANOVA. Cardiovascular, endocrine and other physiological measures were collected but are not presented in this paper; immune results from the trial were published separately (Pacifici et al., 2001).
can_establish: That in 9 healthy men with prior MDMA use, taking MDMA with alcohol, compared with each alone and with placebo in the same people, produced the alcohol-like fall in DSST performance at its peak without the rise in self-rated sedation seen with alcohol alone, with undiminished feelings of drunkenness, MDMA-like euphoria and good effects that lasted longer, an MDMA blood peak 13% higher and an alcohol blood peak 15% lower, under the doses and timing this study chose.
cannot_establish: What the combination does to heart rate, blood pressure or body temperature (measured but not reported here); its effect on driving or on real-world accidents; what happens in women, at other doses, with repeated doses or in hot, crowded settings; or that the combination's impairment equals alcohol's (no equivalence test, 9 people).

sample.recruitment: Men recruited by word of mouth; paid for participation (p. 237, Materials and Methods › Subjects). Seventeen were included in all: 8 in a pilot dose-finding trial (Camí et al., 2000b) and 9 in this study.
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Recreational MDMA use on at least five occasions and previous experience of acute alcohol intoxication; physician interview, physical examination, routine laboratory tests, urinalysis and 12-lead ECG; structured psychiatric interview (SCID) to exclude history or presence of major psychiatric disorders (schizophrenia, psychosis, major affective disorder); no DSM-IV drug abuse or dependence except nicotine; no history of adverse medical or psychiatric reactions to MDMA; all were extensive CYP2D6 metabolizers by dextromethorphan phenotyping (p. 237).
sample.demographics: 9 men; mean age 23 (range 19–36) years; weight 67.4 kg (59–81); height 175 cm (167–183); alcohol 1.6 units a day on average (1 unit = 8 g ethanol); on average 26 previous MDMA experiences (range 5–100); all but two current smokers (p. 237).
sample.attrition: None: all participants finished the study (p. 242).
sample.selection_effects: Nine men with substantial prior MDMA use, no past bad reactions to it and normal CYP2D6 metabolism. Women, people with slower CYP2D6 metabolism, people with heart or psychiatric conditions and people new to MDMA are not represented; experienced participants may tolerate or rate the effects differently.

exposure.measurement: Given in the laboratory: dl-MDMA supplied by the Spanish Ministry of Health and prepared by the hospital pharmacy as identical opaque soft gelatin capsules (purity not stated); alcohol as vodka with tonic water; the placebo drink was tonic water masked with aromatic bitters and lemon juice (p. 237, Drugs). Plasma MDMA and blood alcohol were measured.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Study conditions: one oral dose of MDMA 100 mg or placebo, fasting, at 9:30; alcohol 0.8 g/kg or placebo drink at 10:00, drunk over 15 min; one week between sessions. The doses were chosen from a pilot that tested MDMA 75 and 100 mg and alcohol 0.5 and 0.8 g/kg, and are described by the authors as in the range of recreational use (pp. 236–237).
exposure.polysubstance: Urine tests for opiates, cocaine, amphetamine and cannabis before each session (results not reported); seven of nine smoked tobacco, allowed from 6 h after dosing (p. 237).
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Urine drug screen before each session; overnight fast; no tobacco until 6 h after dosing (p. 237).

comparison.controls: Within-person: MDMA alone, alcohol alone and double placebo in the same 9 men.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable to the within-person comparison; prior drug experience could shape responses but was not analysed.

outcomes.instruments: Computerized DSST (total and correct responses in 90 s); simple reaction time (Vienna Reaction Unit; decision and motor time); Maddox wing (esophoria as extraocular muscle tension, exophoria as relaxation); ARCI, Spanish validated version (PCAG sedation, MBG euphoria, LSD dysphoria and somatic symptoms, BG intellectual efficiency and energy, A amphetamine-like); 23 visual analogue scales of 100 mm (e.g. stimulated, high, drunken, any effect, good effects, liking, content, drowsiness, confusion, perceptual changes, hallucinations); plasma MDMA by GC-MS and blood alcohol by headspace gas chromatography (pp. 237–238).
outcomes.validity_norms: Established laboratory tests; a training period of 4–5 h before the study brought DSST and reaction-time performance to a steady level (p. 237).
outcomes.operationalization: Peak change from baseline in the first 6 h and 6-h area under the curve; impairment as fewer DSST responses or longer reaction time than with placebo; duration as the time points at which a condition differed from placebo.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Tukey post hoc tests within each outcome after a significant ANOVA; no correction across the 32 or more outcomes (DSST total and correct, reaction time, Maddox wing, five ARCI scales, 23 visual analogue scales), each analysed as peak and area.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Double-blind and double-dummy, with the placebo drink masked; whether participants could tell the conditions apart was not assessed.

analysis.effect_sizes: No standard deviations or confidence intervals for the psychomotor and subjective outcomes (means in figures only); F(3,24) values in Table 1. Mean peak DSST differences: alcohol vs placebo −5.89 total and −9.0 correct responses; combination vs placebo −4.89 and −8.11; alcohol vs MDMA −4.78 and −8.11; combination vs MDMA −8.11 correct. ARCI-MBG (euphoria) peak differences: MDMA and combination vs placebo 9.78 and 9.67; vs alcohol 5.33 and 5.22. Pharmacokinetics (Table 2, mean ± SD): alcohol peak 124.62 ± 14.94 mg/dl alone vs 105.81 ± 4.99 with MDMA (p = 0.004); alcohol AUC0–6h 409.08 ± 24.28 vs 371.74 ± 18.67 (p < 0.001); MDMA peak 231.42 ± 36.20 alone vs 260.29 ± 42.22 with alcohol (p = 0.007); MDMA AUC 2447.85 ± 711.81 vs 2345.08 ± 838.35 (p = 0.471). Editors' calculation: MDMA peak +12.5%, alcohol peak −15.1%, alcohol AUC −9.1%, matching the paper's 13%, 15% and 9%.
analysis.preregistration_detail: No trial registration is reported in the paper.
analysis.selective_reporting: Cardiovascular, endocrine and other physiological parameters were evaluated but are explicitly not presented in this manuscript (p. 237), so the heart-rate, blood-pressure and temperature effects of the combination, central to its risks, are not available here. Table 1 lists only variables with significant results, and means appear only in figures.

interpretation_gap.results_show: With MDMA plus alcohol, DSST performance at its peak fell about as much as with alcohol alone, but the fall lasted about 1 h instead of 2–3 h, and the combination's 6-h area did not differ significantly from placebo while alcohol's did; decision time at peak was longer than with placebo only under the combination. Self-rated sedation (ARCI-PCAG) rose with alcohol alone but not with the combination, while feelings of drunkenness were not reduced. Euphoria peaked about as high as with MDMA alone but stayed above placebo for 5.25 h instead of 2.25 h, and good effects, liking and contentment over 6 h were greater than with MDMA alone. MDMA's blood peak was 13% higher and alcohol's 15% lower with the combination.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract says combined use “causes dissociation between subjective and objective sedation” and that people might feel they are doing better while performance stays impaired (p. 236). Perceived performance was not measured, and the combination's objective impairment on the DSST was shorter than alcohol's. The discussion extends this to possible reckless driving and to greater abuse potential than MDMA alone (pp. 243–244), and suggests that the 13% rise in MDMA levels might matter for neurotoxicity, although the authors themselves call the kinetic changes mild and within the range of differences between people (p. 243). The authors do say that confirmation in driving and field studies is needed (p. 244).

timeline.event: Camí et al. (2000b): pilot dose-finding trial of MDMA (75 and 100 mg) with alcohol (0.5 and 0.8 g/kg) in pairs of subjects (n = 8), from which this study's doses were chosen (not read here)
Pacifici et al. (2001), J Pharmacol Exp Ther 296: immune effects of MDMA alone and with alcohol, reported from this trial (not read here)
This paper: presented as the first information in humans on the psychomotor, subjective and pharmacokinetic interaction of MDMA and alcohol

replication.where_it_stands: The authors describe the interaction as not previously studied in humans. Later studies were not part of this reading.

funding.funder: Fondo de Investigación Sanitaria (FIS 97/1198), CIRIT 97-SRG-0077, and Plan Nacional sobre Drogas (p. 236, first-page footnote).
funding.declared_conflicts: No conflict-of-interest statement in the article.
funding.affiliations_note: Institut Municipal d'Investigació Mèdica, Universitat Autònoma de Barcelona, Hospital del Mar and Universitat Pompeu Fabra; the Plan Nacional sobre Drogas is a Spanish government programme. Recorded as a flag for closer reading, not as a reason to discount.

what_would_settle_it: A larger randomized crossover study in women and men giving MDMA and alcohol alone and together at more than one dose, reporting heart rate, blood pressure, body temperature and blood sodium alongside psychomotor tests, with participants' own ratings of how well they think they are performing and a driving-simulator task.

domains.note: Random assignment by a balanced 4 × 4 Latin square is stated; sequence generation and concealment are not described, and nine people cannot fill a 4 × 4 square evenly.
One week between sessions; training before the study brought test performance to a steady level, limiting practice effects.
Double-dummy with a masked placebo drink, but experienced participants are likely to recognise alcohol and MDMA; no check of the blind.
All nine completed; F(3,24) fits complete data.
Self-ratings by participants who may have known their condition; DSST, reaction time and drug levels are objective.

No registration; cardiovascular and endocrine outcomes collected but not reported; Table 1 lists only variables with significant results; the text goes beyond Table 1 in places (see reporting issues).

risk_of_bias.reasoning: The randomized within-person comparison is sound for the psychomotor and subjective measures, with all nine participants completing. Confidence is lowered by the very small all-male sample, the omission of the cardiovascular and endocrine results that were collected, and text statements that go beyond Table 1. The paper may be cited, for 9 healthy men with prior MDMA use at one dose of each drug, for: alcohol-like DSST impairment at peak with the combination but less self-rated sedation, undiminished feelings of drunkenness, longer-lasting MDMA-like good effects, and small changes in blood levels (MDMA peak about 13% higher, alcohol peak about 15% lower). It may not be cited for the combination's effects on heart rate, blood pressure or body temperature, for driving, for women, or as showing that the combination impairs exactly as much as alcohol.

key_findings.finding: Design and sample: 9 healthy men aged 19–36 with on average 26 previous MDMA experiences (range 5–100), all extensive CYP2D6 metabolizers, each received MDMA 100 mg plus alcohol 0.8 g/kg, MDMA alone, alcohol alone and double placebo in random order (balanced Latin square), double-blind and double-dummy, one week apart; the drink was taken over 15 min starting 30 min after the capsules. All completed.
key_findings.locator: Materials and Methods › Subjects; Drugs; Study Design

key_findings.finding: Psychomotor impairment (DSST): at peak, both alcohol conditions reduced DSST responses compared with placebo (mean peak differences: alcohol −5.89 total and −9.0 correct responses; combination −4.89 and −8.11); alcohol's impairment lasted 2–3 h (from 1 h to 3–4 h after dosing) and the combination's 1 h (1–2 h). Over 6 h (area), alcohol differed from placebo but the combination did not; alcohol and the combination did not differ significantly from each other on the DSST or reaction time.
key_findings.locator: Results › Psychomotor Performance, 1st paragraph (p. 238, right column, continuing on p. 239); Table 1 (p. 239)

key_findings.finding: Reaction time: the combination lengthened decision time at peak compared with placebo, the only significant pairwise difference for this measure; in the time course both alcohol conditions lengthened total and decision reaction time at some time points, the combination for half an hour (1–1.5 h after MDMA).

Self-rated sedation (ARCI-PCAG) rose with alcohol alone compared with all other conditions (peak at 2 h, significant from 2 to 4 h); with the combination it stayed at the level of MDMA alone, so MDMA abolished alcohol's subjective sedation. MDMA also reduced alcohol-induced drowsiness ratings but did not change feelings of drunkenness, which were raised by both alcohol conditions compared with placebo or MDMA.
key_findings.locator: Results, 4th paragraph (p. 240, left column) and 7th paragraph (pp. 241–242); Table 1 (p. 239); Fig. 3 (p. 241)
key_findings.note: Approximate peak drunken ratings read from Fig. 3: about 58 mm with the combination and 40 mm with alcohol alone (difference not significant).

key_findings.finding: Euphoria (ARCI-MBG) rose with MDMA and with the combination compared with placebo and alcohol (peak differences 9.78 and 9.67 against placebo, 5.33 and 5.22 against alcohol); compared with placebo it lasted 15 min after alcohol, 2.25 h after MDMA and 5.25 h after the combination, with similar maximal effects for MDMA and the combination.
key_findings.note: MDMA and the combination did not differ significantly in MBG peak or area (Table 1, p. 239); the longer duration comes from the time-course analysis.

key_findings.finding: Over 6 h, the combination scored higher than MDMA alone on the visual analogue scales for good effects, liking and contentment (area, p < 0.05) and drunken, while MDMA alone scored higher on confusion; the combination lengthened these effects by about 1–2 h with similar peak intensity. No condition changed ratings of hallucinations.
key_findings.locator: Results, 7th paragraph (p. 241, right column, continuing on p. 242); Table 1 (p. 239)

key_findings.finding: Eye-muscle balance (Maddox wing): MDMA produced esophoria (eye-muscle tension, which the authors associate with stimulants) compared with placebo and alcohol; alcohol slightly increased exophoria (not significant at peak or area); the combination fell between the two, partly reversing alcohol's exophoria.
key_findings.locator: Results, 3rd paragraph (p. 239, right column, continuing on p. 240)

key_findings.finding: Blood levels (Table 2, mean ± SD; median for time to peak): alcohol peaked at 124.62 ± 14.94 mg/dl alone and 105.81 ± 4.99 mg/dl with MDMA (p = 0.004), with 6-h area 409.08 ± 24.28 vs 371.74 ± 18.67 (p < 0.001) and peak reached at 1.5 vs 2 h (p = 0.014); MDMA peaked at 231.42 ± 36.20 alone and 260.29 ± 42.22 with alcohol (p = 0.007), with no difference in time to peak (1.5 h) or area (2447.85 ± 711.81 vs 2345.08 ± 838.35, p = 0.471). The paper gives these as a 13% higher MDMA peak and 15% lower alcohol peak.
key_findings.note: Table 2 labels the MDMA peak in mg/dl, which cannot be right for these values; the assay range of 25–400 ng/ml (p. 238) indicates ng/ml (see reporting issues).

key_findings.finding: No serious adverse reactions were observed; no participant needed specific treatment or special care during the sessions, and all finished the study.
Cardiovascular, endocrine and other physiological parameters were evaluated in the trial but are not presented in this paper; immune results appeared in Pacifici et al. (2001).
The authors call the kinetic changes statistically significant but mild in magnitude and within the range of differences between individuals, and say they may partly explain the effects observed.

reporting_issues.issue: The text says both alcohol conditions decreased total and correct DSST responses compared with placebo and with MDMA, but Table 1 shows the combination differed from placebo only at peak (not in 6-h area) and from MDMA only in peak correct responses.
reporting_issues.consequence: The combination's psychomotor impairment was shorter and less consistent than the text states.

reporting_issues.issue: The text says MDMA alone increased ARCI-BG (intellectual efficiency and energy) compared with placebo and alcohol, but Table 1 shows MDMA vs placebo not significant (peak and area) and MDMA vs alcohol significant only at peak, and Fig. 2 draws MDMA's BG point as not different from placebo.
reporting_issues.consequence: Only the combination clearly raised BG scores.

reporting_issues.issue: The mean peak DSST differences are internally inconsistent: the alcohol pairs imply MDMA minus placebo = −0.89 correct responses, the combination pairs imply 0 (both printed as −8.11) (editors' calculation).
reporting_issues.consequence: At least one of the printed −8.11 values is probably a copying error; the direction of the findings is unaffected.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 2 labels the peak-concentration column mg/dl for both drugs, but MDMA values of 231–260 must be ng/ml given the assay's 25–400 ng/ml range; its area column is headed AUC0–6h for both drugs while the methods and results give AUC0–24h for MDMA, although MDMA was sampled only up to 10 h; the area units are printed as mg/dl·h⁻¹.
reporting_issues.consequence: The MDMA values cannot be cited with the printed units; the MDMA area's time window is uncertain.

reporting_issues.issue: Cardiovascular, endocrine and other physiological measures were collected but deliberately not presented, and no companion paper is cited for them.
reporting_issues.consequence: The study cannot answer what the combination does to heart rate, blood pressure or temperature, which matter most for its risks.
